Pattern 06 of 21

Monotonic Stack

Keep a stack that is always sorted. The moment a new element breaks the order, everyone it "beats" gets popped, and each popped element learns its answer right then.

1. What is this pattern for?

Picture people standing in a line, all facing right, waiting to see over the crowd. A short person can't see past anyone taller. When a tall person walks up at the back, every shorter person directly in front of them finally gets their answer: "the first person taller than me is that one", and then they leave the line. The people left in line are always arranged tallest at the front, shortest at the back. That line is a monotonic stack.

A monotonic stack is a plain Python list used as a stack, with one rule: its values stay in order (always decreasing, or always increasing, from bottom to top). Before you push a new element, you pop everything that would break the order.

That popping is the useful part. When element x pops element y, you've learned something about y: x is the first element after y that is bigger (or smaller) than it. So the pattern answers "next greater / next smaller / previous greater / previous smaller" for every index in one pass, O(n), instead of the O(n²) "for each element, scan right" brute force.

It's the engine behind a family of famous problems: daily temperatures, stock span, largest rectangle in a histogram, trapping rain water, sum of subarray minimums and "remove digits to make the smallest number".

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Decide what you're looking for. "Next greater" means you keep a decreasing stack (a bigger newcomer pops smaller ones). "Next smaller" means you keep an increasing stack.
  2. Store indices, not values. With an index you can read the value (nums[j]), compute distances (i - j) and write into an answer array (ans[j]).
  3. Walk left to right. For each new element x at index i: while the stack's top is "beaten" by x, pop it and record x (or i) as its answer.
  4. Push i. It now waits on the stack until something beats it.
  5. Leftovers have no answer. Anything still on the stack at the end never found a greater (smaller) element, so it keeps the default (-1, 0, or n).
  6. Why it's O(n): each index is pushed once and popped at most once. The inner while loop looks scary but does at most n pops in total.

The same machine run the other way around: when you want the previous smaller element, keep an increasing stack. After popping, whatever is left on top is the answer for the new element.

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot Monotonic Stack

Trigger words

  • "next greater / next smaller element", "previous greater / smaller"
  • "how many days until a warmer temperature", "stock span", "how far can each person see"
  • "largest rectangle", "maximal rectangle", "trapping rain water"
  • "sum of minimums (or maximums) of all subarrays"
  • "remove k digits / letters to get the smallest (lexicographically) result"

Shape of the input

  • A 1-D array (or string) where order matters and you can't sort it.
  • Each element's answer depends on the nearest element to its left/right that is bigger or smaller.
  • The brute force is "for each i, scan outward until you hit something bigger". That's O(n²).
The one question to ask"For each element, do I need the nearest element on one side that is bigger or smaller than it?" If yes, it's a Monotonic Stack.
Direction cheat-codeLooking for greater → keep the stack decreasing. Looking for smaller → keep it increasing. The stack is always the opposite of what you're hunting for.

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use Monotonic Stack when…Prefer something else when…
You need the nearest greater/smaller element for every indexYou need the k-th largest overall, ignoring position: use Top K Elements (heap)
You need the max/min of a sliding window of size kThat's a monotonic deque: the same idea, popping from both ends. See Sliding Window
Each bar/element "extends" until something smaller blocks it (histograms)The question is about pairs that sum to a target in a sorted array: use Two Pointers
You're building the smallest/largest sequence greedily by deleting charactersYou need range sums, not nearest-bigger: use Prefix Sum
Order of the input must be kept (no sorting allowed)The data is sorted and you're searching for a value: use Modified Binary Search

Cost: O(n) time (each index is pushed and popped at most once) and O(n) extra space for the stack in the worst case (an already-sorted input never pops).

5. The Python template (memorize this)

# A) Next GREATER element to the right: keep a DECREASING stack of indices
def next_greater(nums):
    # answer[i] starts as -1, meaning "nobody bigger shows up to the right"
    answer = [-1] * len(nums)
    # stack holds INDICES whose answer we do not know yet.
    # Their values are decreasing from bottom to top.
    stack = []
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        current = nums[i]
        # While the value on top of the stack is smaller than current,
        # current is the FIRST bigger value that index has seen.
        while len(stack) > 0 and nums[stack[-1]] < current:
            top_index = stack.pop()        # remove the waiting index...
            answer[top_index] = current    # ...and give it its answer
        # i now waits on the stack for its own next greater element
        stack.append(i)
    # Indices still on the stack never found anything bigger: they keep -1
    return answer

# B) Previous SMALLER element to the left: keep an INCREASING stack
def previous_smaller(nums):
    # answer[i] = index of the nearest smaller value to the LEFT of i (-1 if none)
    answer = [-1] * len(nums)
    # stack holds indices whose values are increasing from bottom to top
    stack = []
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        current = nums[i]
        # Values that are >= current can never be the "previous smaller"
        # for current or for anyone after it, so throw them away.
        while len(stack) > 0 and nums[stack[-1]] >= current:
            stack.pop()
        # Whatever survives on top is smaller than current: that is the answer
        if len(stack) > 0:
            answer[i] = stack[-1]
        else:
            answer[i] = -1
        # current may be the "previous smaller" for someone later
        stack.append(i)
    return answer

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Template A, setup: answer = [-1] * len(nums) makes a list with one -1 per element (the default "no bigger value" answer). stack = [] is a plain Python list used as a stack: append pushes on top, pop() removes the top, stack[-1] reads the top without removing it.
  2. Template A, loop: for i in range(len(nums)) visits every index from left to right, and current = nums[i] is the newcomer.
  3. Template A, the while: len(stack) > 0 makes sure the stack isn't empty before we peek at stack[-1]. If the top's value is smaller than current, then current is that index's next greater element, so we pop the index and write the answer. We repeat until the top is not smaller.
  4. Template A, push: stack.append(i) puts the newcomer on the stack, where it waits for its own answer. Because every smaller top was removed first, the stack stays decreasing.
  5. Template B, setup: same shape, but here the answer is an index on the left, and the stack is kept increasing.
  6. Template B, the while: pop every index whose value is >= current. Such a value is no use as a "previous smaller" for current, and current blocks it for everyone further right too.
  7. Template B, record: after popping, the top (if the stack isn't empty) is the nearest strictly smaller value to the left, so answer[i] = stack[-1]; otherwise the answer is -1. Then push i.
  8. Both functions touch each index at most twice (one push, at most one pop), so the total work is O(n) even though there is a loop inside a loop.

The four variants differ only in the comparison and in when you record the answer:

WantStack orderPop while top is…Answer recorded…
Next greaterdecreasing< xfor the popped index
Next smallerincreasing> xfor the popped index
Previous greaterdecreasing<= xfor i, from the top after popping
Previous smallerincreasing>= xfor i, from the top after popping

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "The tall newcomer clears the line"When someone taller arrives, every shorter person in front of them has found their answer and walks away. Whoever is left is always in sorted order.

Picture

A row of buildings at sunset. Walking right, each new tall building "casts its shadow" back over the shorter ones in front of it. Those shorter ones are popped: their next taller building has been found.

Chant

"While top loses, pop and record; then push me."

Direction rule

"Hunt greater, stack falls. Hunt smaller, stack climbs." Store indices, never just values.

7. LeetCode problems, solved step by step

Medium 739. Daily Temperatures ArrayStack

Problem: Given daily temperatures, for each day return how many days you must wait until a warmer day. If there's none, put 0.

Spot it: "wait until a warmer day" = next greater element, but we want the distance, so we store indices.

Key insight: Keep a decreasing stack of day-indices that are still waiting. When a warmer day i arrives, it answers every colder day waiting_day it pops: answer[waiting_day] = i - waiting_day.

Approach:

  1. Create answer = [0] * n. 0 means "no warmer day", the default for days that never get answered.
  2. Walk the days left to right with an empty stack of indices.
  3. While today is warmer than the day on top of the stack, pop that day waiting_day and write answer[waiting_day] = i - waiting_day.
  4. Push today's index. It now waits for its own warmer day.
  5. Days still on the stack at the end keep 0.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def dailyTemperatures(self, temperatures: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        n = len(temperatures)
        # answer[day] = how many days until a warmer day (0 = never gets warmer)
        answer = [0] * n
        # stack holds indices of days still waiting for a warmer day
        stack = []
        for i in range(n):
            today = temperatures[i]
            # Today is warmer than the day on top? Then that day's wait is over.
            while len(stack) > 0 and temperatures[stack[-1]] < today:
                waiting_day = stack.pop()             # day that just found a warmer day
                answer[waiting_day] = i - waiting_day # distance in days
            # Today starts waiting for its own warmer day
            stack.append(i)
        # Days left on the stack never got warmer, so they keep 0
        return answer

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. answer = [0] * n makes a list of n zeros. 0 is the right answer for any day that never sees a warmer day, so we only overwrite days that do.
  2. stack holds day indices (not temperatures) because we need them to compute distances. Their temperatures go down from bottom to top.
  3. For each day i, today is its temperature. stack[-1] is the index on top, so temperatures[stack[-1]] is that day's temperature.
  4. The while loop keeps going as long as the stack is not empty and the top day is colder than today. Each such day has just found its first warmer day: pop it and store the gap i - waiting_day.
  5. When the loop stops, the top (if any) is at least as warm as today, so today has to wait too: stack.append(i).
  6. Return answer; leftover days on the stack keep their 0.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 503. Next Greater Element II ArrayStack

Problem: The array is circular: after the last element comes the first. For each element, return the next greater value when walking forward (wrapping around), or -1.

Spot it: "next greater element" → decreasing stack. "Circular" → the answer for an element near the end may be near the start.

Key insight: Walk the array twice (step from 0 to 2n-1, using step % n). The second lap lets leftover elements find answers at the beginning. Only push indices during the first lap so nothing is answered twice.

Approach:

  1. Fill answer with -1 and start an empty decreasing stack of indices.
  2. Loop step from 0 to 2n - 1 and read current = nums[step % n]. The second lap plays the role of the wrap-around.
  3. While the top's value is smaller than current, pop it and set its answer to current.
  4. Push the index only during the first lap (step < n), so every index waits at most once.
  5. Whatever remains (the maximum, and equal copies of it) keeps -1.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def nextGreaterElements(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        n = len(nums)
        # -1 means "no greater value anywhere around the circle"
        answer = [-1] * n
        # decreasing stack of indices still waiting for an answer
        stack = []
        # Walk the array twice (2 * n steps) to simulate wrapping around
        for step in range(2 * n):
            index = step % n            # % n turns step n, n+1, ... back into 0, 1, ...
            current = nums[index]
            # current answers every smaller value waiting on the stack
            while len(stack) > 0 and nums[stack[-1]] < current:
                top_index = stack.pop()
                answer[top_index] = current
            # Only push during the first lap so each index waits at most once
            if step < n:
                stack.append(index)
        return answer

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. answer starts as all -1 (the answer for anything that never finds a bigger value). stack holds indices waiting for their answer; their values decrease from bottom to top.
  2. step runs from 0 to 2n - 1. index = step % n is the real position: the remainder after dividing by n, so steps n, n+1, ... map back to 0, 1, .... This second lap is how the array "wraps around".
  3. The while loop pops every waiting index whose value is smaller than current and records current as its answer, just like the next-greater template.
  4. if step < n: indices are pushed only during the first lap. In the second lap we only answer leftover indices; pushing again would make them wait twice.
  5. Indices still on the stack at the end (the maximum and its equal copies) keep -1.

Dry run on the example: nums = [1, 2, 1] (n = 3)

stepindexcurrentPoppedPushed?stack afteranswer
001nothingyes[0][-1, -1, -1]
112index 0: answer = 2yes[1][2, -1, -1]
221nothingyes[1, 2][2, -1, -1]
301nothingno (2nd lap)[1, 2][2, -1, -1]
412index 2: answer = 2no (2nd lap)[1][2, -1, 2]
521nothingno (2nd lap)[1][2, -1, 2]

Final answer: [2, -1, 2].

Complexity: O(n) time (2n steps, each index pushed/popped once), O(n) space.

Medium 402. Remove K Digits StringStack

Problem: Given a number as a string and an integer k, delete exactly k digits so the remaining number is as small as possible. Return it without leading zeros ("0" if empty).

Spot it: "remove k characters to get the smallest result" while keeping order. A digit should be deleted when a smaller digit comes right after it. That's "pop the top while it's bigger than the newcomer": an increasing stack.

Key insight: Leftmost digits matter most. Greedily, whenever the top of the stack is larger than the incoming digit and you still have deletions left, pop it. If deletions remain at the end, the stack is non-decreasing, so drop from the tail.

Approach:

  1. Scan the digits left to right, keeping a stack of digits you've decided to keep.
  2. While you still have deletions (deletions_left > 0) and the top digit is bigger than the current digit, pop it and do deletions_left = deletions_left - 1. A smaller digit moving left always shrinks the number.
  3. Push the current digit.
  4. If deletions remain, the stack is non-decreasing, so pop that many digits off the end (the largest ones).
  5. Strip leading zeros. Return "0" if nothing is left.
class Solution:
    def removeKdigits(self, num: str, k: int) -> str:
        # how many digits we are still allowed to delete
        deletions_left = k
        # digits we keep, in non-decreasing order bottom -> top
        stack = []
        for i in range(len(num)):
            digit = num[i]
            # A bigger digit sitting right before a smaller one makes the number
            # bigger, so delete it (as long as we still have deletions left).
            while deletions_left > 0 and len(stack) > 0 and stack[-1] > digit:
                stack.pop()
                deletions_left = deletions_left - 1
            stack.append(digit)
        # Deletions left over: the stack is non-decreasing, so the biggest
        # digits are at the end. Remove them one at a time from the end.
        while deletions_left > 0:
            stack.pop()
            deletions_left = deletions_left - 1
        # Skip leading zeros: move 'start' past every "0" at the front
        start = 0
        while start < len(stack) and stack[start] == "0":
            start = start + 1
        # Build the answer string one character at a time
        result = ""
        for i in range(start, len(stack)):
            result = result + stack[i]
        # Nothing left means the number is zero
        if result == "":
            return "0"
        return result

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. deletions_left is a copy of k that we count down. stack holds the digits (as characters) we have decided to keep.
  2. For each digit, the while loop pops the top digit if we still have deletions, the stack is not empty, and the top is bigger than digit. Comparing single-character strings like "4" > "3" works just like comparing the digits.
  3. Push digit. The stack stays non-decreasing from bottom to top.
  4. After the scan, any remaining deletions are used on the end of the stack, where the largest digits sit (e.g. "112" with k = 1 drops the final 2).
  5. start walks forward past any "0" characters at the front, because a number never shows leading zeros.
  6. The for loop from start to the end glues the remaining digits into result.
  7. If every digit was removed (or all were zeros), result is empty, so return "0".

Dry run on the example: num = "1432219", k = 3

01nothing31
14nothing314
234213
323112
42nothing1122
5120121
69nothing01219

No deletions are left over and there are no leading zeros, so the answer is "1219".

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 907. Sum of Subarray Minimums ArrayStack

Problem: Add up min(sub) over every contiguous subarray of arr. Return the sum modulo 10⁹+7.

Spot it: There are O(n²) subarrays, so enumerating them is too slow. Flip the question: for each element, in how many subarrays is it the minimum? That depends on the nearest smaller element on each side, which is a Monotonic Stack job.

Key insight: If arr[i]'s previous smaller is at L and its next smaller is at R, then any subarray that starts in (L, i] and ends in [i, R) has arr[i] as its minimum. That's (i − L) × (R − i) subarrays. Contribution = arr[i] × (i − L) × (R − i). To avoid double-counting equal values, use "strictly smaller" on one side and "smaller or equal" on the other.

Approach:

  1. For each index i, find L = index of the previous strictly smaller element (−1 if none) with an increasing stack scanned left to right.
  2. Find R = index of the next smaller-or-equal element (n if none) with a second stack scanned right to left. Mixing strict and non-strict counts tied subarrays exactly once.
  3. arr[i] is the minimum of (i − L) × (R − i) subarrays.
  4. Add arr[i] × (i − L) × (R − i) for every i and take the result mod 10⁹+7.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def sumSubarrayMins(self, arr: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        n = len(arr)
        # left_count[i]  = how many choices for the LEFT end where arr[i] is the minimum
        # right_count[i] = how many choices for the RIGHT end where arr[i] is the minimum
        left_count = [0] * n
        right_count = [0] * n

        # Pass 1, left to right: previous STRICTLY smaller element
        stack = []
        for i in range(n):
            # Pop everything >= arr[i]; they are not "strictly smaller"
            while len(stack) > 0 and arr[stack[-1]] >= arr[i]:
                stack.pop()
            if len(stack) > 0:
                previous_smaller = stack[-1]
            else:
                previous_smaller = -1           # nothing smaller on the left
            left_count[i] = i - previous_smaller
            stack.append(i)

        # Pass 2, right to left: next smaller-OR-EQUAL element (tie-break)
        stack = []
        i = n - 1
        while i >= 0:
            # Pop everything > arr[i]; equal values stay and act as a wall
            while len(stack) > 0 and arr[stack[-1]] > arr[i]:
                stack.pop()
            if len(stack) > 0:
                next_smaller_or_equal = stack[-1]
            else:
                next_smaller_or_equal = n       # nothing smaller on the right
            right_count[i] = next_smaller_or_equal - i
            stack.append(i)
            i = i - 1                           # move one step to the left

        # Add up each element's contribution: value * (#left ends) * (#right ends)
        total = 0
        for i in range(n):
            contribution = arr[i] * left_count[i] * right_count[i]
            total = total + contribution
        return total % MOD

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. MOD is 10⁹+7, required by the problem because the sum can be huge. left_count and right_count start as lists of zeros, one slot per element.
  2. Pass 1 (left to right) is the "previous smaller" template. Pop every index whose value is >= arr[i]; what survives on top is the nearest strictly smaller element on the left (or -1 if the stack is empty). left_count[i] = i - previous_smaller is how many start positions (previous_smaller, i] keep arr[i] as the minimum.
  3. Pass 2 (right to left) uses i = n - 1 / while i >= 0 / i = i - 1 to walk backwards. It pops only values that are strictly greater, so an equal value stays as a wall. The survivor is the nearest smaller-or-equal element on the right (or n if none). right_count[i] is how many end positions [i, next_smaller_or_equal) are allowed.
  4. Using "strictly smaller" on one side and "smaller or equal" on the other means a subarray with several equal minimums is counted for exactly one of them.
  5. The final loop multiplies arr[i] × left_count[i] × right_count[i] (value × number of subarrays where it is the minimum), adds everything up, and returns the total mod 10⁹+7.

Dry run on the example: arr = [3, 1, 2, 4] (n = 4)

Hard 84. Largest Rectangle in Histogram ArrayStack

Problem: Bars of width 1 have heights heights[i]. Find the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the histogram.

Spot it: A rectangle that uses bar i as its shortest bar can stretch left and right until it hits a shorter bar. "Nearest shorter on both sides" → an increasing stack.

Key insight: Keep indices with increasing heights. When bar i is shorter than the top, the top bar can't extend past i, so its rectangle is finished: its right wall is i and its left wall is the new top of the stack after popping. Width = i − left − 1. Append a sentinel height 0 at the end to flush everything.

Approach:

  1. Append a sentinel height 0 so every bar gets popped at the end.
  2. Keep a stack of indices whose heights are increasing.
  3. When the current height h is ≤ the top's height, pop the top. Its rectangle can't extend past i.
  4. Its left wall is the new top of the stack (or −1 if empty), so width = i − left − 1. Update best with height × width.
  5. Push i and continue. best holds the answer at the end.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def largestRectangleArea(self, heights: List[int]) -> int:
        # Copy the heights and add a sentinel bar of height 0 at the end.
        # The 0 is shorter than everything, so it pops (finishes) every bar.
        bars = []
        for i in range(len(heights)):
            bars.append(heights[i])
        bars.append(0)
        # stack holds indices whose heights are increasing bottom -> top
        stack = []
        best = 0
        for i in range(len(bars)):
            current_height = bars[i]
            # The top bar cannot stretch past i, so its rectangle is finished
            while len(stack) > 0 and bars[stack[-1]] >= current_height:
                top_index = stack.pop()
                height = bars[top_index]
                # Left wall = first shorter bar to the left (new top), or -1
                if len(stack) > 0:
                    left_wall = stack[-1]
                else:
                    left_wall = -1
                # The rectangle spans the bars strictly between the two walls
                width = i - left_wall - 1
                area = height * width
                if area > best:
                    best = area
            stack.append(i)
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The first loop copies heights into bars (so we don't change the caller's list), then appends a sentinel 0. Because 0 is shorter than every real bar, reaching it pops everything left on the stack, so no bar is forgotten.
  2. stack holds indices of bars with increasing heights. best is the biggest area found so far.
  3. For each bar i, the while loop runs while the bar on top is at least as tall as the current one. That top bar can't extend to the right past i, so its rectangle is complete.
  4. top_index = stack.pop() removes it; height is its height, which is the height of its rectangle.
  5. After popping, the new top (if any) is the nearest shorter bar on the left: the left wall. If the stack is empty, the rectangle reaches the very start, so we use -1 as the wall.
  6. width = i - left_wall - 1 counts the bars strictly between the two walls. area = height * width; keep it if it beats best.
  7. Push i. The stack stays increasing.

Dry run on the example: heights = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] (so bars = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3, 0])

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

8. Common mistakes

Storing values instead of indicesYou can't compute distances (739), widths (84) or write ans[j] from a value alone. Push indices and read nums[stack[-1]].
Wrong direction of the stackHunting "greater" needs a decreasing stack. If your stack grows the same way as what you hunt, nothing ever pops.
< vs <= with duplicatesDecide whether equal values count as "greater". In counting problems (907), use strict on one side and non-strict on the other, or you'll double-count.
Forgetting the leftoversElements still on the stack at the end never got an answer. Either rely on the default value or flush them with a sentinel (the extra bar of height 0 appended in problem 84).
Checking an empty stackAlways write while len(stack) > 0 and ... (or the short form while stack and ...). Reading stack[-1] on an empty list raises IndexError.

9. Self-check quiz

To find the next greater element for every index, the stack's values (bottom → top) should be…

A bigger newcomer pops the smaller tops, so whatever remains is decreasing. "Hunt greater, stack falls."

The code has a while loop nested inside a for loop. What's the total time complexity?

Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the inner loop runs at most n times in total across the whole scan (amortized analysis).

"For each building, how many buildings to its right can it see before a taller one blocks the view?"

"Before a taller one" = next greater element. That's the decreasing stack.

"Return the maximum of every window of size k." Which variant fits best?

You need to pop old indices from the front when they leave the window and smaller values from the back. A deque does both in O(1) (LeetCode 239).

Every problem in the table that isn't solved in section 7 is worked out below. Click a problem name in the table to jump to it.

Easy 496. Next Greater Element I ArrayStackHash Map

Problem: nums1 is a subset of nums2 (all values distinct). For each value in nums1, find the first greater value to its right in nums2, or -1.

Spot it: "Next greater element" is the template word for word. The only twist is that answers are looked up by value, so store them in a dict.

Approach:

  1. Scan nums2 with a decreasing stack of values.
  2. When current is bigger than the top, pop the top and record next_bigger[top] = current.
  3. Push current.
  4. Answer each query in nums1: look it up in next_bigger, or use -1 if it was never popped.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def nextGreaterElement(self, nums1: List[int], nums2: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        # next_bigger[value] = first bigger value to its right in nums2
        next_bigger = {}
        # decreasing stack of VALUES (allowed because the values are distinct)
        stack = []
        for i in range(len(nums2)):
            current = nums2[i]
            # current is the first bigger value for every smaller value on top
            while len(stack) > 0 and stack[-1] < current:
                smaller_value = stack.pop()
                next_bigger[smaller_value] = current
            stack.append(current)
        # Answer each query; values never popped have no bigger value (-1)
        answer = []
        for i in range(len(nums1)):
            value = nums1[i]
            if value in next_bigger:
                answer.append(next_bigger[value])
            else:
                answer.append(-1)
        return answer

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. next_bigger is a dictionary that maps a value to the first bigger value after it in nums2. We key by value (not index) because the queries in nums1 are values.
  2. stack holds values still waiting for a bigger value; they are decreasing from bottom to top. Storing values instead of indices is safe here only because all values are distinct.
  3. For each current in nums2, the while loop pops every smaller value on top and records current as its answer. It is the first bigger value each of them has met.
  4. Push current; it now waits for its own bigger value.
  5. The second loop builds the answer for nums1. If a value is in next_bigger, use that; otherwise it was never popped, so nothing bigger came after it: use -1.

Dry run on the example: nums1 = [4, 1, 2], nums2 = [1, 3, 4, 2]

icurrentPopped (value → answer)stack afternext_bigger
01nothing[1]{}
131 → 3[3]{1: 3}
243 → 4[4]{1: 3, 3: 4}
32nothing[4, 2]{1: 3, 3: 4}

Queries: 4 is not in the dictionary → -1; 1 → 3; 2 is not in the dictionary → -1. Final answer: [-1, 3, -1].

Complexity: O(n + m) time, O(m) space.

Medium 901. Online Stock Span Stack

Problem: Prices arrive one per day. For each new price, return its span: how many consecutive days, ending today and going backwards, had a price ≤ today's.

Spot it: "Going backwards until a bigger price" means you need the previous greater element, in a stream. A decreasing stack that remembers how many days each entry already covers answers it.

Approach:

  1. Keep a stack of (price, span) pairs with strictly decreasing prices.
  2. On a new price, start with span = 1 (today).
  3. While the top's price is ≤ today's, pop it and add its span. Those days are all covered by today now.
  4. Push (price, span) and return span.
class StockSpanner:
    def __init__(self):
        # Each entry is a pair (price, span). Prices are strictly decreasing
        # from bottom to top.
        self.stack = []

    def next(self, price: int) -> int:
        span = 1                                   # today always counts
        # Every earlier price <= today is covered by today's span.
        # Its span already counts the days IT covered, so add them all at once.
        while len(self.stack) > 0 and self.stack[-1][0] <= price:
            top_pair = self.stack.pop()
            top_span = top_pair[1]                 # index 1 = the span part
            span = span + top_span
        self.stack.append((price, span))
        return span

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. __init__ creates an empty stack. Each entry will be a pair (price, span); pair[0] is the price and pair[1] is the span.
  2. next(price) starts with span = 1 because today itself always counts.
  3. self.stack[-1][0] is the price of the top entry. While it is <= price, that day (and every day it already covered) is part of today's span, so we pop it and add its span to ours. We never need those days again: today is at least as high and blocks them.
  4. Push (price, span) so later days can absorb today's whole run in one step, then return span.

Dry run on the example: calls next(100), next(80), next(60), next(70), next(60), next(75), next(85)

Complexity: Amortized O(1) per call (each day is pushed and popped once), O(n) space.

Medium 1081. Smallest Subsequence of Distinct Characters StringStackHash Set

Problem: Return the lexicographically smallest subsequence of s that contains every distinct letter exactly once. (Same as LeetCode 316.)

Spot it: "Smallest result" built by deleting characters while keeping order is the same greedy as Remove K Digits: an increasing stack. The extra rule is that you can only drop a letter if it appears again later.

Approach:

  1. Record last_index[letter], the last index of each letter.
  2. Scan s. Skip letter if it's already on the stack.
  3. While the top is bigger than letter and appears again later (last_index[top] > i), pop it. You'll pick it up again later, in a better spot.
  4. Push letter and mark it as used. Glue the stack into a string at the end.
class Solution:
    def smallestSubsequence(self, s: str) -> str:
        # last_index[letter] = last position where that letter appears.
        # Later positions overwrite earlier ones, so we end with the last one.
        last_index = {}
        for i in range(len(s)):
            letter = s[i]
            last_index[letter] = i
        stack = []          # letters of the answer, built left to right
        used = set()        # letters currently on the stack
        for i in range(len(s)):
            letter = s[i]
            if letter in used:
                continue    # each letter appears only once in the answer
            # Drop a bigger letter on top if it shows up again later
            # (we can re-add it later in a better position).
            while len(stack) > 0 and stack[-1] > letter and last_index[stack[-1]] > i:
                removed_letter = stack.pop()
                used.remove(removed_letter)
            stack.append(letter)
            used.add(letter)
        # Glue the letters together into one string
        result = ""
        for i in range(len(stack)):
            result = result + stack[i]
        return result

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The first loop fills last_index. Each time a letter is seen, its entry is overwritten with the current position, so at the end it holds the last position of every letter.
  2. stack is the answer being built; used is a set that answers "is this letter already on the stack?" instantly.
  3. In the main loop, a letter that is already used is skipped with continue: the answer must contain each letter exactly once.
  4. The while loop pops the top letter if three things are true: the stack is not empty, the top letter is bigger than the current one (so putting the current letter earlier makes the string smaller), and the top letter appears again later (last_index[...] > i), so it is safe to drop it now and add it back later. A popped letter is also removed from used.
  5. Push the current letter and mark it as used.
  6. The last loop glues the stacked letters into one string, left to right.

Dry run on the example: s = "bcabc", so last_index = {'b': 3, 'c': 4, 'a': 2}

4cnothingabc

Final answer: "abc".

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (at most 26 letters).

Medium 456. 132 Pattern ArrayStack

Problem: Return True if there are indices i < j < k with nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j] (small, big, middle).

Spot it: For each candidate "3" (nums[j]), we want the largest "2" to its right that is smaller than it. That's a previous/next-greater relationship, so use a monotonic stack scanned from the right.

Approach:

  1. Scan from right to left, keeping a decreasing stack and third = the best "2" seen so far (starts at −∞).
  2. If the current value is less than third, it's a valid "1". Return True.
  3. While the top is smaller than the current value, pop it into third. The current value is a "3" that sits to the left of the popped "2".
  4. Push the current value. If the scan ends, return False.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def find132pattern(self, nums: List[int]) -> bool:
        # third = best "2" found so far (it has a bigger "3" to its left)
        third = float("-inf")
        # decreasing stack of values, filled while scanning right -> left
        stack = []
        i = len(nums) - 1
        while i >= 0:
            current = nums[i]
            # current < third means: current ("1") < third ("2") < some "3"
            if current < third:
                return True
            # current is a "3" for every smaller value on top; they become "2" candidates
            while len(stack) > 0 and stack[-1] < current:
                third = stack.pop()
            stack.append(current)
            i = i - 1                       # move one step to the left
        return False

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. third starts at minus infinity (float("-inf"), smaller than every number), meaning "no valid 2 found yet".
  2. i = len(nums) - 1 and while i >= 0 walk the array from the last index down to 0. i = i - 1 at the bottom of the loop moves one step left.
  3. If current < third, then current is the "1": it sits to the left of a "3" and a "2" with 1 < 2 < 3. Return True.
  4. Otherwise, the while loop pops every value smaller than current. Each popped value has a bigger value (current) to its left, so it is a valid "2". Because the stack is decreasing, the last value popped is the biggest such "2", which gives the best chance of finding a "1" later.
  5. Push current; it may serve as a "3" or a "2" for values further left.
  6. If the scan finishes without finding a "1", return False.

Dry run on the example: nums = [3, 1, 4, 2] (scanning right to left)

244 < -inf? no. Pop 2 (smaller than 4), so third = 2.2[4]
111 < third=2: return True2[4]

Final answer: True (the pattern is 1, 4, 2).

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Hard 42. Trapping Rain Water ArrayStack

Problem: Bars of width 1 have heights height[i]. How much rain water is trapped between them after it rains?

Spot it: Water collects in a "valley": a lower bar with a taller bar on each side. When a taller bar arrives, it closes the valleys of the shorter bars before it. That's "pop while the top is smaller".

Approach:

  1. Keep a stack of indices with decreasing heights.
  2. When height[i] is taller than the top, pop the top. That bar is the valley's bottom.
  3. If the stack is now empty, there's no left wall, so stop. Otherwise the new top is the left wall.
  4. Water layer = (min(left wall, current) − bottom) × (i − left − 1). Add it.
  5. Push i. (A two-pointer version also works in O(1) space.)
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def trap(self, height: List[int]) -> int:
        # stack holds indices whose heights are decreasing bottom -> top
        stack = []
        water = 0
        for i in range(len(height)):
            current_height = height[i]
            # A taller bar closes the valley of the shorter bar on top
            while len(stack) > 0 and height[stack[-1]] < current_height:
                bottom = stack.pop()                  # the valley floor
                if len(stack) == 0:
                    break                             # no left wall: water spills out
                left_wall = stack[-1]
                # Water rises to the LOWER of the two walls
                if height[left_wall] < current_height:
                    water_level = height[left_wall]
                else:
                    water_level = current_height
                depth = water_level - height[bottom]
                width = i - left_wall - 1
                water = water + depth * width         # one horizontal layer of water
            stack.append(i)
        return water

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. stack holds indices of bars with decreasing heights (each one could be the left wall of a future pool). water is the running total.
  2. For each bar i, the while loop runs as long as the bar on top of the stack is shorter than the current bar. That shorter bar is the floor of a valley whose right wall is bar i.
  3. bottom = stack.pop() takes the floor off the stack. If the stack is now empty there is no left wall, so water would spill out: break.
  4. Otherwise the new top is the left wall. Water can only rise to the lower of the two walls, so water_level is the smaller of height[left_wall] and current_height.
  5. depth is how far that level is above the floor, and width is the number of columns strictly between the walls. depth * width is one horizontal slab of water, added to the total.
  6. After the pops, push i. It may be the left wall of a later pool.

Hard 85. Maximal Rectangle MatrixStack

Problem: In a binary matrix of "0"/"1", find the area of the largest rectangle containing only 1s.

Spot it: Treat each row as the floor of a histogram: bar c = how many consecutive 1s stand above (and including) this row in column c. Each row is then exactly problem 84.

Approach:

  1. Keep heights[c]. For each row, set it to heights[c] + 1 if the cell is "1", otherwise 0.
  2. Run the Largest Rectangle in Histogram stack algorithm on heights.
  3. Track the best area over all rows.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def maximalRectangle(self, matrix: List[List[str]]) -> int:
        if len(matrix) == 0:
            return 0
        column_count = len(matrix[0])
        # heights[j] = number of consecutive "1"s ending at the current row in column j
        heights = [0] * column_count
        best = 0
        for i in range(len(matrix)):
            row = matrix[i]
            # Grow or reset each column's bar for this row
            for j in range(column_count):
                if row[j] == "1":
                    heights[j] = heights[j] + 1
                else:
                    heights[j] = 0
            # Problem 84 on this row's histogram
            area = self.largest(heights)
            if area > best:
                best = area
        return best

    def largest(self, heights: List[int]) -> int:
        # Same as problem 84: copy the bars and add a sentinel 0
        bars = []
        for i in range(len(heights)):
            bars.append(heights[i])
        bars.append(0)
        stack = []          # indices, heights increasing
        best = 0
        for i in range(len(bars)):
            current_height = bars[i]
            while len(stack) > 0 and bars[stack[-1]] >= current_height:
                top_index = stack.pop()
                height = bars[top_index]
                if len(stack) > 0:
                    left_wall = stack[-1]
                else:
                    left_wall = -1
                width = i - left_wall - 1
                area = height * width
                if area > best:
                    best = area
            stack.append(i)
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. An empty matrix has no rectangle, so return 0 right away.
  2. heights has one bar per column. heights[j] counts how many "1"s stand in an unbroken column ending at the current row.
  3. For each row i, the inner loop updates every column j: a "1" makes the bar one taller, a "0" knocks it down to 0 (a rectangle of 1s can't pass through a 0).
  4. After updating, heights is a histogram whose floor is this row. self.largest(heights) finds the biggest rectangle in it, and we keep the best area over all rows.
  5. largest is exactly problem 84: copy the bars, add a sentinel 0, keep an increasing stack of indices, and every time a bar is popped compute height × (i − left_wall − 1).

Hard 239. Sliding Window Maximum ArrayDeque

Problem: Return the maximum of every contiguous window of size k as it slides from left to right.

Spot it: Each window's max is "the biggest element that hasn't been beaten by a later, bigger one". That's a monotonic structure, but old indices also leave from the front, so use a deque.

Approach:

  1. Keep a deque of indices whose values are decreasing from front to back.
  2. For each new x, pop from the back while the back's value is ≤ x. Those values can never be a window max again.
  3. Append i. If the front index has slid out of the window (≤ i − k), pop it from the front.
  4. Once i ≥ k − 1, the front's value is the current window's maximum.
from collections import deque
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def maxSlidingWindow(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> List[int]:
        # A deque is a list that is fast to change at BOTH ends:
        #   append(x) adds at the back, pop() removes from the back,
        #   popleft() removes from the front, window[0] reads the front.
        # It holds indices whose values are decreasing front -> back.
        window = deque()
        result = []
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            current = nums[i]
            # Values <= current can never be a window maximum again
            while len(window) > 0 and nums[window[-1]] <= current:
                window.pop()
            window.append(i)
            # The front index slid out of the window [i - k + 1, i]
            if window[0] <= i - k:
                window.popleft()
            # Once the first full window is reached, the front is the maximum
            if i >= k - 1:
                result.append(nums[window[0]])
        return result

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. window = deque() creates a double-ended queue. Unlike a plain list, removing from the front (popleft()) is instant. It stores indices, and the values at those indices go down from front to back.
  2. result = [] collects one maximum per window.
  3. The for loop visits every index i; current = nums[i] is the new value entering the window.
  4. The while loop removes indices from the back whose values are <= current. While current is in the window, those smaller, older values can never be the maximum, and they will leave the window before current does.
  5. window.append(i) puts the new index at the back. The deque is still decreasing.
  6. The window covers indices i - k + 1 to i. If the front index is <= i - k, it has slid out, so popleft() removes it. At most one index leaves per step.
  7. Once i >= k - 1 we have a full window, and the front of the deque holds the index of its maximum, so we append nums[window[0]].

Dry run on the example: nums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3

13pop back 0[1] (values [3])[]
2-1nothing[1, 2] (values [3, -1])[3]
3-3nothing[1, 2, 3] (values [3, -1, -3])[3, 3]
45pop back 3, pop back 2, pop back 1[4] (values [5])[3, 3, 5]
53nothing[4, 5] (values [5, 3])[3, 3, 5, 5]

Complexity: O(n) time (each index enters and leaves the deque once), O(k) space.

Medium 853. Car Fleet ArrayStack

Problem: n cars drive toward target on a one-lane road. Car i starts at position[i] with speed[i]. A faster car that catches a slower one ahead must slow down and drive with it as one fleet. How many fleets arrive at the target?

Spot it: Process cars from closest-to-target to farthest. Each car's solo arrival time is (target − pos) / speed. A car behind can only stay separate if it arrives later than the fleet ahead. That's a stack whose times strictly increase.

Approach:

  1. Pair positions with speeds and sort by position, descending (nearest the target first).
  2. For each car compute time = (target − pos) / speed.
  3. If the stack is empty or time is greater than the top's time, this car can't catch the fleet ahead: push it as a new fleet.
  4. Otherwise it catches up and merges into that fleet (don't push; the fleet keeps the slower, later time).
  5. The stack's size is the number of fleets.
class Solution:
    def carFleet(self, target: int, position: List[int], speed: List[int]) -> int:
        # pair each car's position with its speed, nearest-to-target first
        cars = sorted(zip(position, speed), reverse=True)
        # arrival times of the fleets ahead, slowest (latest) on top
        stack = []
        for pos, spd in cars:
            time = (target - pos) / spd
            if not stack or time > stack[-1]:
                # can't catch the fleet ahead before the target: a new fleet
                stack.append(time)
            # else: it catches up and joins the fleet ahead (nothing to push)
        return len(stack)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. sorted(zip(position, speed), reverse=True): zip pairs each position with its speed, and sorting the pairs by position, descending, puts the car nearest the target first.
  2. time = (target - pos) / spd: how long this car would take on its own.
  3. if not stack or time > stack[-1]: the fleet directly ahead arrives at stack[-1]. If this car needs more time, it never catches up: it leads a new fleet.
  4. If time <= stack[-1], the car catches the fleet ahead at or before the target and is slowed to its pace, so it adds no fleet.
  5. return len(stack): one entry per fleet.
